text: Ἠργμένον τὸ κακόν· οὐχ ἠργμένον τὸ ἀγαθόν. Cœptum malum ; bonum non cœptum ; cujus utriusque clara ratio Maximo tradita : quod malum a nobis nostraque sit voluntate ; bonum autem in tota sua latitudine abstrahat ab eo quod est cœpisse ; quod sit bonum natura, ipsum æternum Deusque. Insipide Picus et ἀφιλοσόφως, malum coarctatum, bonum non arctatum.
anchorLine: ἀγαθόν (g)· πρὸ παντὸς γὰρ αἰῶνος καὶ χρόνου, φύ-
readNote: the note is set across the full width, its Latin running on into the right half
en: 'Begun is the evil; not begun the good.' The evil begun, the good not begun. The clear reason for each was handed down by Maximus: that evil is from us and from our own will, while good, in its whole breadth, withdraws from the fact of having begun, since it is good by nature, itself eternal and God. Picus (renders it) insipidly and unphilosophically: 'evil confined, good not confined.'

text: Τοῦ κατόπιν ὑπερφερούς. Τὸ, ὑπερφερές, Hesych. μέγα, ὑπὲρ φύσιν, ὑπεράγον. Idem proinde hic Maximo, atque τὸ κρεῖττον· virtus scilicet, et quod naturam excedit, nobisque a Deo est, potentia sua roborante nostram infirmitatem. Quem virtutis ὅρον sapientissime hic statuit Maximus κατ᾿ ἐπίγνωσιν, ut nempe sic agnoscamus vereque sentiamus, nancisci nos virtutem non nostris viribus, sed in hoc Deo nobis vires præstante, ut nec per defectum, pusilli animi simus; nec per excessum, superbi. Sic, cap. 71, egregie distincta Maximo τὰ τῶν ἔργων καὶ νοημάτων ψυχικὰ καὶ πνευματικά· clariusque, cap. 72, exposita divisio illa ψυχῆς καὶ πνεύματος, quam in nobis facit divinus Sermo; virtutum scilicet quarum ex natura rationes habemus, et quarum ex spiritu, divino munere gratiam accipimus. Erat editis, ὑπερφερὴς πα[...] ἑαυτῷ γινόμενος, redditque Picus, seipsum pi[...]lentem faciens et quod est a tergo. Quod durius est.
anchorLine: πλημμελῶν, ὡς τοῦ κατόπιν ὑπερφερούς (i) παρ᾿ ἑαυ-
readNote: set across the foot of both columns (left column to 'divino munere', right continues 'gratiam accipimus'); the printed letters of ὑπερφερ- are worn in the note, so it is read as 'ὑπερφερ-' in each occurrence; two worn spans are written [...]
en: On 'of what is behind (him), exceeding'. Hesychius: 'ὑπερφερές' = great, beyond nature, exceeding. The same, then, here in Maximus, as 'the better' (τὸ κρεῖττον): namely virtue, which exceeds nature and is ours from God, its power strengthening our weakness. Maximus most wisely sets down here the definition of virtue 'according to knowledge': that we so acknowledge and truly feel that we obtain virtue not by our own strength but in this, God supplying us strength, so that we are neither faint-hearted through defect nor proud through excess. So in chapter 71 Maximus distinguishes well 'the things of works and thoughts that are of the soul and of the spirit'; and more clearly in chapter 72 he sets out the division of soul and spirit that the divine Word makes in us: that is, of the virtues of which we have the reasons by nature and of those of which we receive grace by the gift of the Spirit. The editions had 'ὑπερφερὴς πα[...] ἑαυτῷ γινόμενος', and Picus rendered it 'making himself [...]lent and what is behind (him)'. Which is harsher still.

text: Τοῦ ταύτης χρῄζοντος. Hoc ipsum superiori cap. dixerat, Ὁ τῆς εὐχῆς τοῦ δικαίου δεόμενος, quo utroque loco Picus, Qui opus habet oratione Justi, cui est necessaria. At Maximus cap. 83 et [...]4 de petitione melius exponit, qua peccator justi precum suffragia imploret; quæ est proxima ratio orandi pro eo, et altera earum vocum significatio; ipsa non abhorrens a priore, sed ex illa orta: ex eo enim quod egeamus, rogamus qui possit indigentiam levare. Sæpe Chrys. illos exagitat, qui suam ipsi vitam negligentes, aliorum precibus salutem se adep[...]uros sp[...]rant.
anchorLine: ταύτης χρῄζοντος (j), πλέον τῶν ἀρετῶν ἡδομένῳ
readNote: the chapter number after 'cap. 83 et' has a worn first digit (reads like S4); two letters of 'adep…uros' and of 'sp…rant' are worn
en: On 'of him who needs this (prayer)'. He had said the same in the preceding chapter, 'he who needs the prayer of the just man', where in both places Picus renders 'He who has need of the prayer of the Just, to whom it is necessary'. But Maximus in chapters 83 and [...]4 explains better the petition by which a sinner implores the support of the prayers of the just; this is the nearest sense of praying for him and the second meaning of those words, not at odds with the first but arising from it: for from the fact that we are in need we ask one who can relieve the want. Chrysostom often upbraids those who, themselves neglecting their life, hope to obtain salvation through the prayers of others.
